figures.title: Three kinds of shock
figures.caption: All three lower blood pressure and urine output; the heart rate, skin, neck veins and lungs tell them apart. Cardiogenic shock is the one where a large fluid bolus makes the client worse.
rows: Blood or fluid loss: hemorrhage, burns, vomiting, diarrhea
Pump failure: large MI, severe heart failure, dysrhythmia
Vessels dilate: sepsis, anaphylaxis, spinal cord injury (neurogenic)
Fast and thready, the earliest sign; BP holds until late
Warm and flushed early; warm and dry in neurogenic shock
Clear; wheezes or stridor in anaphylaxis
Stop the bleeding; rapid isotonic fluids or blood
Oxygen, inotropes, reperfusion; no large fluid boluses
Fluids and vasopressors; antibiotics for sepsis, IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis

figures.title: Sepsis: the first hour
figures.caption: Start every step within the first hour: each hour antibiotics are delayed raises the risk of death. Cultures come before antibiotics, but never hold the antibiotic up.

steps.title: Spot it early
steps.detail: Infection plus a fast heart rate and breathing, fever or a low temperature, low BP or new confusion. An older adult may show only confusion.

steps.title: Measure lactate
steps.detail: Above 2 mmol/L means tissues are underperfused. Remeasure within 2 to 4 hours if it is high; a falling lactate means treatment is working.

steps.title: Blood cultures before antibiotics
steps.detail: Two sets from two sites, drawn first so the organism can be found, but never let them delay the first dose.

steps.title: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
steps.detail: Within 1 hour of recognition. Narrow the drug later, once culture and sensitivity results return.

steps.title: Fluids: 30 mL/kg for low BP or lactate
steps.detail: For hypotension or a lactate of 4 or more, give 30 mL/kg of normal saline or lactated Ringer's within 3 hours. A 70 kg adult gets 2,100 mL.

steps.title: Vasopressors to a MAP of 65 or higher
steps.detail: If BP stays low with fluids, start norepinephrine, peripherally if no central line is ready yet, for a mean arterial pressure of 65 or higher.

steps.title: Reassess perfusion
steps.detail: Improving: MAP 65 or higher, urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/hr, falling lactate, clearer thinking, faster capillary refill.

figures.title: Left- vs right-sided heart failure
figures.caption: Left backs up into the lungs, right into the rest of the body. Daily weight is the best check on fluid: report a gain of 2 to 3 lb (about 1 kg) in a day or 5 lb (2.3 kg) in a week.
rows: Dyspnea, orthopnea, waking breathless at night
Less breathless; the signs show in the body
Crackles, cough, pink frothy sputum in pulmonary edema
Fatigue, confusion, low urine output, S3 heart sound
Neck vein distension, dependent edema, weight gain, enlarged liver, ascites
MI, hypertension, aortic or mitral valve disease
Left-sided failure, COPD (cor pulmonale), pulmonary hypertension
High Fowler's, oxygen, IV diuretic, watch potassium
Daily weight, sodium limit, skin care over swollen legs

figures.title: Cardiac markers after an MI
figures.caption: Troponin is the marker of choice: specific to heart muscle and high for up to 2 weeks. Draw it on arrival and repeat it, because one early normal result does not rule out an MI.

series.label: Myoglobin
series.note: First to rise, within 1 to 3 hours, and normal again within about a day. It is in all muscle, so it is not specific to the heart.

series.label: CK-MB
series.note: Rises in 3 to 6 hours, peaks at 12 to 24 hours, normal in 2 to 3 days, so a fresh rise after that points to a new infarction.

series.label: Troponin I or T
series.note: Most specific to heart muscle. Rises in 3 to 6 hours, peaks around 24 hours, stays high 7 to 14 days, so it catches a late MI.

figures.title: Suspected MI: first actions
figures.caption: The ECG and aspirin come first. Oxygen is for a saturation below 90%, not for everyone, and nitroglycerin can crash the BP of a client who is hypotensive or took an erectile dysfunction drug.

steps.title: Stop, rest and call for help
steps.detail: Stay with the client, sit them up in semi-Fowler's, and call the rapid response team or 911. Take vital signs and SpO2.

steps.title: 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes
steps.detail: ST elevation means a STEMI and starts the reperfusion clock. Start an IV and draw a troponin at the same time.

steps.title: Aspirin, chewed
steps.detail: 162 to 325 mg of non-enteric-coated aspirin, chewed so it works faster, unless the client is allergic or actively bleeding.

steps.title: Oxygen only if SpO2 is below 90%
steps.detail: Routine oxygen does not help a client whose saturation is normal. Give it for SpO2 below 90% or respiratory distress.

steps.title: Nitroglycerin, if BP allows
steps.detail: 0.4 mg sublingual every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses. Hold for systolic BP below 90 or a PDE-5 inhibitor (sildenafil) taken within 24 to 48 hours.

steps.title: Reperfusion
steps.detail: STEMI: PCI with door-to-balloon within 90 minutes, or a fibrinolytic within 30 minutes of arrival if PCI is not available.

figures.title: Increased intracranial pressure
figures.caption: A change in level of consciousness is the earliest sign. Cushing triad comes late and means the brainstem is being compressed. Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees and the neck midline.
rows: Restless, irritable or newly confused: the first sign
Hard to arouse, then unresponsive; Glasgow score 8 or below
Fixed and dilated on one side, then both
Cushing triad: rising systolic BP, wide pulse pressure, slow pulse, irregular breathing
New weakness or drift on one side
Headache, vomiting, blurred or double vision
Seizures, loss of gag and corneal reflexes
Head of bed 30 degrees, neck midline, quiet room, space out care, prevent straining
Call the provider at once: herniation may be close. Protect the airway.

figures.title: Glasgow Coma Scale
figures.caption: Add the best eye, verbal and motor responses. 15 is fully alert and 3 is the lowest possible score. A score of 8 or below means the client cannot protect the airway; a drop of 2 points is a change to report.
rows: 4: confused. 3: inappropriate words. 2: sounds only. 1: none
5: localizes pain. 4: withdraws. 3: abnormal flexion. 2: extension. 1: none
3 is the lowest. 8 or below: coma; protect the airway

figures.title: Stroke: left vs right hemisphere
figures.caption: Deficits land on the side opposite the damaged hemisphere. With a field cut, put things in the seeing field at first, then teach the client to turn the head and scan the blind side.
rows: Aphasia: trouble speaking (expressive), understanding (receptive) or both
Slow and cautious, aware of deficits, often anxious or depressed
Right-sided field loss in both eyes
Left field loss, left neglect, misjudges distance
Short phrases, yes-or-no questions, gestures, picture board; allow time
Brief step-by-step cues; check each task is done safely
Call light and items on the unaffected left side at first
Close supervision, bed alarm, cue to scan to the left
Chair on the stronger left side; lead with the left leg
Chair on the stronger right side; lead with the right leg
Screen swallowing before any food, fluid or pills
Same risk: eat fully upright, chin tucked, small bites

figures.title: Acute stroke: the first hour
figures.caption: Time lost is brain lost. The last known well time decides alteplase, the CT must rule out bleeding first, and nothing goes by mouth until the client passes a swallow screen.

steps.title: Call a stroke alert
steps.detail: Sudden face droop, arm drift, slurred speech, vision loss or loss of balance. Activate the stroke team and score a stroke scale (NIHSS).

steps.title: Establish the last known well time
steps.detail: When the client was last seen normal, not when found. It decides whether alteplase can be given.

steps.title: Check glucose; keep NPO
steps.detail: Low glucose can mimic a stroke. Nothing by mouth, not even aspirin or pills, until bleeding is ruled out and a swallow screen is passed.

steps.title: Noncontrast head CT, stat
steps.detail: It must rule out bleeding before any clot-dissolving drug. Aim to start imaging within 20 minutes of arrival.

steps.title: BP below 185/110 and no exclusions
steps.detail: Screen for active bleeding, recent head trauma or brain surgery, and anticoagulant use. Lower the BP first if it is too high.

steps.title: Alteplase within 4.5 hours
steps.detail: IV bolus, then a 60-minute infusion, within 4.5 hours of last known well. Aim for 60 minutes or less from door to needle.

steps.title: Watch for bleeding in the brain
steps.detail: Neuro checks and BP every 15 minutes at first; keep BP at or below 180/105. Severe headache or drowsiness: stop the infusion and call.

figures.title: Chest tube troubleshooting
figures.caption: Keep the unit below the chest and the tubing free of loops. Don't strip the tube or clamp it except briefly to find a leak. Brief water-seal bubbles as a client with a pneumothorax coughs are expected.
rows: Normal: rises on inhaling, falls on exhaling (reversed on a ventilator)
Nothing; it shows the system is open to the chest
Nothing; if it stops, check the suction source
Lung has re-expanded, or the tubing is kinked, clotted or looped
Check for kinks and loops; report so an x-ray can confirm
Air leak in the client or the system
Check the dressing and connections from the chest down; report a new leak
Drainage above 100 mL/hr or bright red
Notify the provider at once; check BP and heart rate
Blocked tube; after heart surgery, possible tamponade
Check the tubing, never strip it; low BP with distended neck veins: call at once
Air can be drawn into the chest
Reconnect cleanly at once; if the unit broke, put the tube end 2 to 5 cm in sterile water
Sterile occlusive dressing taped on 3 sides; assess breathing; call the provider

figures.title: Oxygen delivery devices
figures.caption: Match the device to how much oxygen the client needs and how exact it must be. Titrate to the SpO2 target, not to 100%, and keep smoking, flames and sparks away: oxygen feeds fire.
rows: Client can eat and talk. Humidify above 4 L/min; pad the ears and check the nares
Never below 5 L/min, or the client rebreathes exhaled carbon dioxide
Most precise. Choose it when an exact percentage is prescribed, as in COPD
Highest without intubation. Keep the reservoir bag from collapsing on inhaling
Heated and humidified; for acute respiratory failure
Low flow, often 1 to 2 L/min, or Venturi 24% to 28%
Target SpO2 88% to 92%. New drowsiness can mean carbon dioxide is building up

figures.title: Major burns: the first 24 hours
figures.caption: Airway comes before fluids: soot, singed nasal hair or hoarseness means the airway can swell shut within hours. Parkland's first 8 hours count from the time of the burn, not from arrival.

steps.title: Stop the burning
steps.detail: Remove smoldering clothing and all jewelry before swelling starts. Cool water only for small burns; cover large burns and keep the client warm.

steps.title: Airway: look for inhalation injury
steps.detail: Soot at the mouth or nose, singed nasal hair, hoarseness, stridor or facial burns: give 100% oxygen and prepare for early intubation.

steps.title: Suspect carbon monoxide
steps.detail: Headache and confusion after a fire. Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal, so check carboxyhemoglobin and keep 100% oxygen by nonrebreather.

steps.title: Estimate the burn size
steps.detail: Adult rule of nines: head 9%, each arm 9%, front 18%, back 18%, each leg 18%, perineum 1%. Count partial and full thickness only.

steps.title: Parkland: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA
steps.detail: Lactated Ringer's over 24 hours; %TBSA is the percent of skin burned. Half in the first 8. 80 kg, 40%: 12,800 mL; 6,400 mL (800 mL/hr) by hour 8.

steps.title: Titrate to urine output
steps.detail: Aim for 0.5 mL/kg/hr, about 30 to 50 mL/hr in an adult. Less means more fluid is needed; much more risks fluid overload.

steps.title: Pain, warmth and infection control
steps.detail: IV opioids (IM absorbs poorly), a warm room, sterile dressing technique, tetanus if due. Check pulses under circumferential burns.

figures.title: Neutropenia: precautions and fever
figures.caption: With few neutrophils, an infection may show only as fever, with no pus and little redness. So treat any fever as an emergency, and keep infection sources out of the room.

steps.title: Check the ANC
steps.detail: WBC × (% neutrophils + % bands) ÷ 100. Below 1,000/mm3 calls for neutropenic precautions; below 500 the infection risk is severe.

steps.title: Private room, clean hands
steps.detail: Strict hand hygiene; positive-pressure, HEPA-filtered room after a stem cell transplant. No fresh flowers, plants or standing water.

steps.title: Remove other infection sources
steps.detail: No raw meat, eggs or unwashed produce. No rectal temperatures, suppositories or enemas. Keep ill visitors and staff away.

steps.title: Check temperature often
steps.detail: Fever may be the only sign. A temperature of 38 C (100.4 F) or higher, or chills, is reported at once.

steps.title: Fever: cultures, then antibiotics
steps.detail: Draw blood cultures, from any central line and a vein, then give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

steps.title: Teach for home
steps.detail: Hand hygiene, avoid crowds and sick contacts, no live vaccines, no litter boxes or bird cages, call for a fever of 100.4 F (38 C).

figures.title: Sickle cell crisis
figures.caption: Dehydration, cold, low oxygen and infection make red cells sickle and block small vessels. Relieve pain fast and fully, hydrate, keep warm, and treat new chest pain with fever as acute chest syndrome.

topics: Pain Assessment in Sickle Cell Disease

steps.title: Treat pain fast, on a schedule
steps.detail: IV opioids within 1 hour of arrival, then around the clock or by PCA, not as needed. Believe the client's pain rating.

steps.title: Hydrate
steps.detail: IV and oral fluids ease sickling. Listen to the lungs: too much fluid can bring on acute chest syndrome.

steps.title: Oxygen if SpO2 is below 95%
steps.detail: Treat hypoxemia, which drives sickling; oxygen for a normal saturation does not end a crisis.

steps.title: Warmth, not cold
steps.detail: Warm packs and a warm room. Cold narrows vessels and worsens sickling, so never apply ice.

steps.title: Watch for acute chest syndrome
steps.detail: New chest pain, fever, cough or falling SpO2: report at once. Incentive spirometry every 2 hours while awake helps prevent it.

steps.title: Watch for stroke and sequestration
steps.detail: Sudden weakness or speech change means stroke. In a child, a rapidly enlarging spleen with pallor and low BP is an emergency.

steps.title: Prevent the next crisis
steps.detail: Plenty of fluids; avoid cold, high altitude and overexertion; keep vaccines current; take hydroxyurea as prescribed.

figures.title: Upper GI bleed: first actions
figures.caption: The first sign of a large bleed is usually a rising heart rate, not a falling BP or hemoglobin. Circulation comes first: two large IVs and volume before the search for the source.

steps.title: Recognize the bleed
steps.detail: Coffee-ground or bright red vomit, black tarry stools, dizziness on standing and a climbing heart rate. NSAIDs and ulcers are common causes.

steps.title: Protect the airway
steps.detail: Turn the client to the side or raise the head of the bed so vomited blood is not aspirated. Keep the client NPO.

steps.title: Two large-bore IVs
steps.detail: 18 gauge or larger. Draw a type and crossmatch, CBC, clotting studies and BUN at the same time.

steps.title: Restore volume
steps.detail: Isotonic crystalloid first, then packed red cells as prescribed, usually for a hemoglobin below 7 g/dL (8 with heart disease).

steps.title: Stop the bleeding
steps.detail: IV proton pump inhibitor as prescribed and endoscopy within 24 hours. Variceal bleeding adds octreotide and banding.

steps.title: Monitor closely
steps.detail: Vital signs, orthostatic changes, output and stools. Hemoglobin lags behind acute loss; a high BUN with a normal creatinine means digested blood.

figures.title: Tamponade vs tension pneumothorax
figures.caption: Both squeeze the heart: low BP, distended neck veins and a racing pulse. Listen to tell them apart. Muffled heart sounds point to tamponade; absent breath sounds on one side point to tension pneumothorax.
rows: Blood or fluid fills the sac around the heart: heart surgery, chest trauma, pericarditis
Air trapped in the pleural space: chest trauma, ventilator, blocked chest tube
Shifts away from the affected side (a late sign)
Pulsus paradoxus; chest tube drainage may stop suddenly
Uneven chest rise, rising ventilator pressures, low SpO2
Pericardiocentesis, or a return to surgery after heart surgery
Needle decompression, then a chest tube
